planting.note: Direct sow in hills after last frost once soil has warmed past 65°F; this heirloom needs a full warm season to ripen and benefits from black plastic mulch or row cover in cooler climates to speed early growth.

directions: Sow seeds an inch deep in enriched, well-drained hills spaced a yard apart, keeping soil evenly moist until vines establish and then easing off water as fruit ripens to concentrate sugars. Green Nutmeg is a 19th-century American heirloom muskmelon named for its ribbed, netted rind, which resembles the wrinkled shell of a nutmeg seed and sets it apart from smoother-skinned melon types of the same era. The pale green flesh is notably sweet and aromatic for an old variety, ripening to a musky perfume that signals harvest readiness alongside the classic full slip from the vine. It is a good choice for gardeners wanting an old American melon type distinct from the many French and Charentais heirlooms already common in seed catalogs.

common_name: Prescott Fond Blanc Melon (White-Bottomed French Cantaloupe)
scientific_name: Cucumis melo var. cantalupensis 'Prescott Fond Blanc'

planting.note: Direct sow or transplant after all frost danger has passed and soil is reliably warm; this heavily ribbed French heirloom needs a long, hot summer to fully sugar up, so gardeners in short-season climates should start plants indoors 3-4 weeks early.

directions: Start seed indoors in short-season regions or direct sow into warm soil after frost, spacing vines generously to allow good air circulation and reduce fungal disease pressure. Prescott Fond Blanc is a traditional French market melon named for its deep, warty ribbing and the pale, creamy patch, or fond blanc, where the fruit rests on the ground as it ripens. The orange flesh is dense, sweet, and highly perfumed, and the variety has long been prized in Provençal markets as one of the most flavorful of the old French cantaloupe types. Harvest when the stem begins to crack and separates cleanly from the fruit, the classic slip stage that signals full sweetness.

common_name: Queen Anne's Pocket Melon (Dudaim Melon, Pomegranate Melon)

planting.note: Direct sow after last frost in average garden soil; the compact vines need less space than standard melons and can be grown in containers or trained along a small trellis.

directions: Sow an inch deep in warm soil after frost danger passes, and let vines ramble along the ground or train them up a light trellis, since the fruit is small and light enough not to need slings. This heirloom, grown in Victorian and earlier gardens more for its intense perfume than for eating, produces palm-sized striped orange-and-yellow fruit that was traditionally carried in a pocket or reticule to scent a room or a handkerchief drawer. The flesh is edible but mild and mealy rather than sweet, so most modern gardeners grow it as a fragrant curiosity and conversation piece rather than a dessert melon. It is closely related to modern snake melons and has been kept in circulation mainly by heirloom seed stewards for its novelty and historical interest.

common_name: Long Pie Pumpkin (New England Long Pie Squash)

planting.note: Direct sow in hills after last frost, giving vines ample room to run; the elongated fruit needs a long, dry curing period after harvest for maximum storage life.

directions: Plant seeds in hills of two or three after frost danger passes, and let the long vines sprawl since the fruit is too heavy and elongated to trellis practically. Long Pie is an old New England heirloom, cylindrical rather than round, growing two to three feet long and resembling an overgrown zucchini more than a typical jack-o'-lantern pumpkin. Its smooth orange rind and dense, mild-flavored flesh make it a traditional substitute for butternut or sugar pumpkin in pies and baking, and its thick shell allows it to store for many months longer than most winter squash. Harvest before hard frost when the rind resists a fingernail scratch, then cure in a warm, dry spot for a week or two before moving to cool winter storage.

planting.note: Direct sow 2-4 weeks before last frost for a spring crop, or in late summer for fall; can be harvested young as baby leaf or allowed to form full loose heads.

directions: Broadcast or row-sow seed shallowly in fertile, well-drained soil, thinning to a foot apart for full heads or leaving plants closer together for repeated baby-leaf cuts. Bronze Arrow forms an upright, loose, romaine-like rosette of narrow, pointed leaves that emerge green at the base and deepen to a rich bronze-red at the tips and edges, especially in cool weather and strong sun. It is notably slow to bolt and holds good quality longer into warm weather than many heirloom lettuces, making it a dependable choice for extending the spring lettuce season. The arrow-shaped leaves and striking two-tone coloring also make it a popular addition to mixed salad plantings for looks as well as flavor.

planting.note: Direct sow 2-4 weeks before last frost, or again in late summer for a fall crop; thin seedlings as they grow to give each head room to fully form.

directions: Sow seed shallowly in cool, moist soil and thin plants as they grow to give each head room to fill out. Grandpa Admire's is an Ozark family heirloom lettuce preserved and distributed by Seed Savers Exchange, forming a loose, semi-heading rosette that bridges the gap between a butterhead and a romaine in both leaf shape and texture. The pale green leaves are tender and mild-flavored with a buttery crunch, and the variety is valued for holding in the garden without turning bitter longer than many spring lettuces. As a passed-down heirloom with a documented family origin, it is a good choice for gardeners interested in preserving lesser-known regional lettuce lines.

planting.note: Direct sow as soon as soil can be worked in spring, or in late summer for a fall crop; keep the seedbed consistently moist since carrot seed germinates slowly.

directions: Sow seed thinly and shallowly in loose, stone-free soil, thinning seedlings to a few inches apart once true leaves appear so roots have room to size up. Belgian White is a long, tapered, white-skinned and white-fleshed heirloom carrot historically grown across Europe as a large, productive dual-purpose root for both the table and livestock feed. The roots often push up out of the soil as they mature, developing a green shoulder where exposed to light, and can grow considerably larger than typical orange table carrots while staying reasonably tender. Its mild, less sweet flavor compared to orange carrots and unusual coloring make it a distinctive choice for gardeners wanting to diversify beyond the standard Nantes and Danvers types already common in home gardens.

planting.note: Direct sow after last frost in warm soil, or start indoors 2-3 weeks early for an earlier harvest; pick fruit small and often to keep vines productive.

directions: Direct sow seed an inch deep in fertile, well-drained soil after frost danger has passed, providing a trellis or light support to keep fruit clean and straight. De Bourbonne is a traditional French heirloom from the Burgundy region bred specifically for pickling, producing short, blocky, black-spined fruit typically harvested at two to four inches long for classic French-style cornichons and gherkins. The vigorous vines set fruit prolifically over a long season, and frequent picking is essential since the cucumbers mature quickly and turn seedy and bitter if left too long on the vine. Its small size and firm, crisp texture make it well suited to whole-fruit pickling rather than fresh slicing.
